result.summary: The Trojans mourn Hippolochus' son, whom Apollo rescues from the pyre, while the Argives grieve for Achilles. Thetis arrives and sets out prizes for the funeral games, and the heroes compete in races, wrestling, boxing, archery, throwing, leaping and chariot and horse racing.

scenes.title: Apollo rescues the Lycian hero
scenes.summary: Apollo snatches the Lycian captain from his pyre and has the winds carry him to Lycia, where a monument and a stream are made for him.
scenes.stakes: The fallen hero's body would be burned to ashes unhonoured.

scenes.title: Trojans rejoice, Argives mourn
scenes.summary: The Argives grieve for Achilles while the Trojans exult, though a wiser Trojan fears Aias, Tydeides and the Atreidae.
scenes.stakes: The Trojans risk false confidence while the Argive leaders remain dangerous.

scenes.title: Hera rebukes Zeus
scenes.summary: The gods are divided, and Hera reproaches Zeus for helping Troy; he answers nothing but broods on Troy's coming fall.
scenes.stakes: Zeus's favour for Troy is questioned, and Hellas faces coming ruin.

scenes.title: Argives wait for Thetis
scenes.summary: The Argives sup, sleep and rise, and Tydeus' son wants to attack, but Aias says they must await Thetis and her prizes.
scenes.stakes: Aias is unaware that death follows soon after the games.

scenes.title: Nestor's song for Thetis
scenes.summary: Thetis arrives and sets prizes; Nestor sings of her wedding and of Achilles' deeds, and she rewards him with horses.

scenes.title: The footrace
scenes.summary: Teucer and Aias son of Oileus race, but a god trips Teucer near the end and Aias wins.
scenes.stakes: Teucer loses the prize and is injured.

scenes.title: Wrestling of Tydeides and Aias
scenes.summary: Tydeides and Aias son of Telamon wrestle evenly until Nestor stops them; Thetis gives them four handmaids.
scenes.stakes: Victory and honour in the wrestling.

scenes.title: The boxing
scenes.summary: Idomeneus wins by default; Nestor shames the young men, and Epeius and Acamas box to a draw and receive silver bowls, then are healed by Podaleirius.
scenes.stakes: Injury and glory in the boxing.

scenes.title: Archery, weights, jumping, javelin
scenes.summary: Teucer wins the archery, Aias hurls the iron bar and wins Memnon's arms, and others win leaping and javelin prizes; no one dares box Aias.
scenes.stakes: Honour in each contest; Aias's rivals fear his strength.

scenes.title: Chariot and horse races
scenes.summary: Menelaus wins the chariot race and Agamemnon outraces Sthenelus on horseback; Thetis gives gifts to all, and Ulysses sits out from his wound.
scenes.stakes: Victory and prizes; Sthenelus' horse swerves.

alias_notes.explanation: Son of Cronos, a title of Zeus.
Patronymic of Diomedes, who is not named in this translation.

notable_quotes.reason: Extended simile likening Troilus' death to a scythed blossom.

analysis.text: Funeral games turn grief into honourable rivalry, with competitors reconciling after fierce contests.
The games echo the funeral of Patroclus in the Iliad, and the poem imitates Homeric epic conventions.

legacy.text: Quintus of Smyrna's funeral games for Achilles recast Homer's Iliad Book 23 and influenced later epic.

fun_facts.text: The poem is by Quintus of Smyrna, a Greek epic poet of the 3rd or 4th century AD, who continued Homer's Iliad.

language_notes.text: Hippolochus' son is Glaucus, Lycian ally of Troy, killed earlier in the war. Here he is given a hero's funeral by the Trojans.
The stream's name Glaucus links the spring to the dead hero, explaining a Lycian landmark by his memory (an aetiological tale).
Cronion means son of Cronus, a title of Jove (Zeus). 'Vouchsafed' means graciously granted.
'I trow' is archaic for 'I believe'; 'breathing-space' means a pause for rest.
'Besprent' is archaic for sprinkled or spattered; the spear is spattered with blood.
'I wot' means 'I know'; 'Achaea's sons' are the Greeks, here called Argives and Danaans too.
Tydeides is Diomedes, son of Tydeus. Atreus' sons are Agamemnon and Menelaus, the Greek leaders.
"Dole" means grief or sorrow; "stalwart Danaans" are the sturdy Greeks, here the Argives besieging Troy.
"Fain would speed Troy to a happy goal" means those gods eagerly wished to bring Troy to a fortunate outcome.
Refers to the wedding of Peleus and the sea-goddess Thetis on Mount Pelion, attended by the gods; their son was Achilles.
"Clamorous guest" figures hunger as an insistent visitor; "ye" addresses the reader generally.
The "starry Bears" are the constellations Ursa Major and Minor; their turning marks the approach of dawn.
"Icarian" refers to the Icarian Sea, part of the Aegean near the island of Icaria.
"Battle-biders" means those who stand firm in battle.
"I trow" means "I believe"; "by this" means by now.
"Meet it is" means it is fitting; the sense is that honouring the dead is owed even if the gods did not will the death.
"Bride of Peleus" is Thetis, the sea-goddess who married the mortal Peleus; "lo" simply draws attention to her arrival.
"At her best" means at her command; "sable-stoled" means wearing a black robe.
"Eld" is archaic for old age. "Neleus' son" is Nestor, the aged king of Pylos.
"Laertes' glorious son" is Ulysses, famed for eloquence; even he yielded to Nestor in debate. "Folkmote" is an assembly.
"Willsomeness" is an unusual coinage meaning charm or alluring quality; "Nereids" are the sea-nymph daughters of Nereus.
"Maunds" are baskets; "ambrosia" is the food or drink of the gods that confers immortality.
The list recalls Achilles' victims, including Telephus, Cycnus ("Cyenus"), Hector, Penthesileia and Memnon, the "son of Dawn" who is not named.
Telephus was wounded by Achilles' spear and healed by rust from that same spear, so he gave Achilles the horses in gratitude.
Kine are cattle, here cows; the archaic plural is used for the prize herd.
Victory-fain means eager for victory; 'fain' is archaic for willing or glad.
Girded themselves with loin-cloths: the runners wore only a cloth around the waist, as in early Greek athletics.
Trammelled means hampered or tangled, as if in a net; the runner's foot is hindered by a supernatural force.
Drave is an archaic past tense of 'drove'.
Leeches here means physicians, not the bloodsucking worm.
Tydeus' son is Diomedes, called Tydeides in this translation; the patronymic names him by his father.
"Ankle-lock" and "hip" refer to wrestling holds: Tydeides slips his hip under Aias, lifts him, and frees his thigh from the hold.
"Third last fall" means the deciding third fall; wrestling matches were won by taking the best of three falls.
"Aweless" means fearless, not awed by anything; here it describes the heroes who were nonetheless amazed.
"Bare" is an old past tense of "bear", meaning carried; the fourth maid cleared away the feast.
Patroclus took these horses from Sarpedon's side when he killed him at Troy, as told in the Iliad; Sarpedon was a Lycian ally of Troy.
Nestor recalls the funeral games for Pelias, king of Iolcus, and his own earlier victories over Ancaeus and the Epeians at Amaryncus' tomb.
"Battle-blenchers" means men who flinch from battle; "thews" are muscles or bodily strength.
Epeius built the Wooden Horse that brought Troy's fall; "not long thereafter" looks ahead to that event.
"Sooth" means truly; the line says they needed little urging to fight.
"To wot" means to know or find out; "limber and lithe" means supple and flexible.
"Welkin" is an old poetic word for the sky.
"Myriad-pored" describes sponges with countless tiny holes.
"Suasion" means persuasion; "placable" means willing to be calmed or forgiving.
Theseus abandoned Ariadne, Minos' daughter, on the isle of Dia (Naxos); Dionysus then took her as his bride.
Oileus' son is the lesser Aias, named after his father; the text later just says Aias, which can blur him with the greater Aias, son of Telamon.
Helm means helmet; the crest of plumes is the target, so the shot must cut the hair-crest off.
Peleus' bride is Thetis, the sea-goddess mother of Achilles, who presents the prizes at these funeral games.
Goodlihead means beauty or comeliness; 'reft' means took away by force.
The Destroyer Fate lured him on: Troilus's death is presented as destiny drawing him into a war he was too young for.
Antaeus was a giant wrestler, son of Earth, defeated by Hercules, who lifted him off the ground and crushed him.
The Nereid is Thetis, one of the sea-nymph daughters of Nereus.
Cycnus, a Trojan ally, killed Protesilaus, the first Greek to leap ashore at Troy, before Achilles killed him.
The Aeacid hero is Achilles, grandson of Aeacus; his mother is Thetis.
Strife of hands and feet means boxing; 'thews' are muscles.
'To-break' is archaic, meaning to smash utterly; 'meed' means reward or portion.
"Ear-lords" is a odd compound for charioteers, the lords of the cars. "Tempest-looted" suggests steeds begotten by or seized from the storm-winds.
Pelops won Hippodameia by beating her father Oenomaus in a chariot race at Elis; Oenomaus had killed earlier suitors who lost to him.
Eetion was Andromache's father, king of Thebe, killed and plundered by Achilles earlier in the war.
The "Altar-star" is a constellation, the Altar, whose rising was believed to bring storms at sea.
Arion was the divine horse said to be born of Poseidon in some tellings; here the poet makes the West-wind his sire and a Harpy his dam.
"Son of the old war-lord, Laertes" is a roundabout way of naming Ulysses; "Aeacas' son" is Achilles, whose death is the occasion for the games.

context_notes.text: The Dardanian gate was a gate of Troy, named for the Trojans' ancestor Dardanus.
Lycia was a region in south-west Asia Minor and Glaucus' homeland. Apollo, a Trojan-favouring god, has the winds carry him there.
Apollo Silverbow is the archer god, a protector of Troy who was said to have guided the arrow that killed Achilles.
Hera, wife of Zeus, favours the Greeks. She reminds him of his own part in arranging Thetis's marriage to the mortal Peleus.
Tydeus' son is Diomedes, one of the leading Greek warriors at Troy.
Thetis, Achilles' sea-goddess mother, is to bring prizes for the funeral games held in honour of her dead son.
Aias (Ajax), son of Telamon, later dies after the contest over Achilles' armour at these games, hence the doom mentioned.
Funeral games for Achilles are being held; Thetis, his mother, sets the prizes in his honour.
The wedding of Peleus and Thetis on Mount Pelion was attended by gods; Cheiron the centaur lived there. It was a famous mythic celebration.
Achilles' son Neoptolemus was being raised on Scyros; the Greeks needed him to take Troy.
Thetis is a sea-goddess and mother of Achilles, whose funeral games are being held; she provides the prizes.
Aias son of Oileus led the Locrians and is distinct from Aias son of Telamon; Teucer is half-brother of the latter and a famed archer.
The Queen of Rivalry is Eris-like Strife, personified as the spirit that spurs competitors.
Nestor is the oldest Greek counsellor, often called on to settle disputes. Achilles has just died and been buried, so these are funeral games.
Thetis is a sea goddess and Achilles' mother. She gives the prizes in honor of her dead son.
Briseis was Achilles' captive woman, taken in the raids around Troy; Lesbos was an island city sacked by him.
Thetis, Achilles' sea-goddess mother, supplies the prizes for his funeral games.
Nestor, son of Neleus, is the oldest Greek leader at Troy and often recalls his youthful feats.
Acamas, son of Theseus, fights with the Greeks at Troy.
Podaleirius is a physician son of Asclepius, the healer god, and serves the Greek army.
These are funeral games for Achilles, with prizes drawn from his spoils. Teucer is the great archer and half-brother of the greater Aias.
Troilus was a young son of Priam and Hecuba, killed by Achilles. Hecuba was queen of Troy.
Hercules and Peleus once sacked Troy under King Laomedon, which explains the history of the bar.
These are funeral games held for Achilles, with chariot races, horse races and prizes given out by his mother Thetis.
Podaleirius was a Greek physician, son of Aesculapius, who treated the wounded.
Sthenelus was a Greek warrior, companion of Diomedes, and son of Capaneus.

literary_notes.text: Apollo's rescue of the body lifts Glaucus above ordinary mortals and shows the gods shaping the war's aftermath.
Comparing grief for Achilles to grief for a son shows how deeply the whole Greek army loved him.
The spear is described as maddened, as if the weapon itself raged, conveying Achilles' terrifying battle fury.
The wise Trojan's warning undercuts the boasting; the reader knows Troy will still fall to the Greeks left alive.
Gods hiding their heads in mountain-like clouds shows their grief through a physical image.
Zeus's silence and brooding show his grim, far-seeing power, brushing aside Hera's reproach.
Sleep is shown as a gentle being who loosens the chain of care from the weary men.
The stirring army is compared to a wind-driven sea and to wind-rippled grain, conveying restless, massed motion.
The narrator hints at Aias's coming death, adding irony to his confident speech.
Thetis's silent, gentle arrival is compared to the still breath of dawn, suggesting her grace and divinity.
Nestor's unmatched speech, to which even Ulysses and Agamemnon defer, establishes his wisdom and authority.
Repeated "sang" builds a rhythmic catalogue and conveys the splendor of the wedding.
The long list of Achilles' victims and qualities magnifies his heroism in epic fashion, though the listeners already know it.
The runners are compared to falcons leaving the line, conveying their speed and eager aggression.
Teucer's trip by an unnamed god or demon suggests divine interference, anticipating Aias's later fate of offending the gods.
Aias darts past 'exultant', showing his triumphant, perhaps unsympathetic character, while his followers share a sudden joy.
Two wrestlers are compared to famished lions fighting over a stag, stressing their equal strength and ferocity.
Fighting mountain-bulls, with echoing hills and dripping foam, make the clash seem elemental and almost cosmic.
Cracking backs and necks are likened to storm-lashed trees knocking their boughs together, adding sound and force.
The wrestlers' kiss and forgotten strife show the heroes' sportsmanship and the bond among the Greeks in their grief.
Nestor's shaming speech shows him as a proud, nostalgic elder who uses his past glory to spur the young.
Epeius is compared to a lion, stressing his fierce, confident bearing as he steps into the ring.
The boxers' clash is likened to storm clouds colliding with lightning and roaring winds, conveying overwhelming force.
A general maxim about wise men closes the reconciliation, giving the narrator's moral view of the draw.
Troilus's death is compared to a gardener cutting a flower before it seeds, stressing his youth, beauty and the waste of his life.
Aias flinging the bar like a dry bough conveys how effortless the throw is for him.
The history of the bar gives it a heroic lineage, tying Aias's feat to Hercules and Achilles.
Fear that his hands would shatter an opponent's face exaggerates Aias's strength and explains why no one will fight him.
Thetis seeing her dead son in Aias's stature ends the scene on grief amid the triumph.
Comparing the speed of the horses to the Harpies, the storm-spirits, conveys their violent, snatching swiftness.
The horses fly so fast that they leave no wheel-track or hoofprint, an exaggeration of speed.
The rising dust is likened to smoke and to mist driven by storm winds, giving the race an elemental scale.
The riders are compared to the winds Boreas and Notus raising the sea, linking their speed to nature's violence.
The crowd's roar is compared to the sea, matching the sound of the throng to a natural force.
